short: Constantine and Licinius agree that Christians, and everyone else, may worship as they choose.
full:
The Edict of Milan was an agreement reached between Constantine and Licinius in early 313 and published as instructions to provincial governors. It restored confiscated church property and granted freedom of worship — not to Christians alone, but to all, in terms deliberately broad enough to cover any religion.

It did not make Christianity the state religion; that came later, under Theodosius. What it did was end the persecution that Diocletian had begun a decade earlier, and put the emperor on the side of a church that had spent three centuries as an illegal association. Within two years Constantine was arbitrating its internal disputes, and by 325 he was convening the Council of Nicaea.

Strictly, the toleration edict of Galerius in 311 came first, and no single document titled "the Edict of Milan" survives. The name has stuck because the settlement it describes is the point at which the empire's relationship with Christianity reverses.
